identity.title: Microbial Rhodopsins: Structural-Functional Mechanisms and the Design of Optogenetic Silencing Tools-With Emphasis on Halorubrum Archaeorhodopsins.

content.abstract: Microbial rhodopsins are light-sensitive membrane proteins that use retinal as a covalent chromophore and adopt a seven-transmembrane alpha-helical fold. They are widely distributed across archaea, bacteria, algae, and fungi and mediate diverse functions, including light-driven ion transport, light-gated ion conduction, and photosensory signaling. Since the discovery of bacteriorhodopsin in 1971, the microbial rhodopsin family has expanded continuously, and channelrhodopsin-based optogenetics has revolutionized neuroscience by enabling millisecond-scale optical control of neuronal activity. However, compared with excitatory tools, optogenetic silencing tools have developed more slowly and remain limited by insufficient photosensitivity, poor membrane localization, ion-homeostasis perturbation, and phototoxicity. Because these properties are largely constrained by the structural and functional features of the parent microbial proteins, the discovery and in-depth characterization of natural rhodopsins remain essential for tool innovation. This narrative review focuses on ion-pumping archaeorhodopsins, with emphasis on the genus Halorubrum and on HeAR, and describes how the literature was selected. We first summarize the functional classification, structural basis, photocycle, and ion-pumping mechanisms of microbial rhodopsins. We then discuss the diversity of Halorubrum archaeorhodopsins and the structural-functional features of HeAR, a recently characterized archaeorhodopsin from a halophilic archaeon isolated from Ejinoor Salt Lake in Inner Mongolia, China. HeAR absorbs at 550 nm (dark-adapted) and 560 nm (light-adapted), essentially the same maximum as AR3 (559 nm). Its Schiff-base counterion Asp-95 has a pKa of 3.5 +/- 0.1, about one unit higher than BR Asp-85 ( approximately 2.6) and AR3 Asp-95 (2.5 +/- 0.2), but matched by AR4 Asp-85 (3.6); thus, this is a property that HeAR shares with its closest relative rather than one that sets it apart. Its photocycle ( approximately 100 ms) is prolonged-roughly ten times longer than the overall cycle of BR (11 ms), of AR4 ( approximately 10 ms) and of the O-decay of AR3 (tau  approximately  14 ms)-while its M intermediate forms and decays faster than in BR; relative to AR3 and AR4, however, the M decay is slower (3.3 ms against  approximately 390 micros and 0.55/3 ms) and the overall cycle is longer. These are established in vitro properties of the heterologously expressed protein, and because a pump moves a fixed, small number of charges per photocycle, low-light performance remains a hypothesis to be tested rather than a demonstrated advantage. In this review "red-shifted" is used in one sense only: HeAR's 550-560 nm window lies  approximately 80-90 nm to the red of excitatory channelrhodopsins ( approximately 470 nm); relative to BR it is blue-shifted by  approximately 18 nm, and relative to AR3 the two absorption maxima coincide. We further review the evolution of optogenetic silencing tools, from inward chloride pumps and outward proton pumps to light-gated anion channels and potassium channels, and discuss structure-guided rational design strategies, including structure prediction, molecular dynamics simulation, directed evolution, and machine learning-assisted engineering. Finally, we outline current challenges and future opportunities in phototoxicity, deep-tissue light delivery, clinical translation and the exploitation of halophilic archaeal resources, and we specify which experiments are required before HeAR can be judged as a silencing tool. Clinically validated optogenetics is kept separate throughout from speculative applications of newly characterized archaeorhodopsins. This review aims to provide a comparative framework linking the structural-functional properties of natural rhodopsins to the rational design of next-generation optogenetic silencing tools.
